newsitem.title: GREECE: Focus - Athens bourse freezes company's assets.
newsitem.headline: Focus - Athens bourse freezes company's assets.

text.p: Brokerages stopped all trade at the Athens bourse on Friday after the exchange clearing house failed to pay cash settlements to several brokers on Thursday.
Brokers said they had no confidence they would be paid by the clearing house unless the bourse acted quickly to sort out the mess.

Bourse officials then announced they were freezing the bank accounts and assets of Delta Securities, and sealing its offices after Delta was found to be in the red with the bourse clearing house for 2.6 billion drachmas.
"The shares of Delta's clients were counted and frozen, the company's offices and safe were sealed," the bourse supervisor's office said in a statement.
The supervisor's office was assisted by the financial crimes division (YPEDA) at the finance ministry, it said.
It also asked court authorities to ban Delta officials from leaving the country. Court sources told Reuters earlier that senior Delta officials would be banned from leaving Greece.
Athens brokerages stopped trading at the bourse on Friday after the clearing house failed to pay several members.
The bourse also said that its clearing house had also frozen whatever Delta assets it held. The stock exchange will continue to monitor daily brokerage trades, it said.
It was the first official statement by the bourse since the settlement upheaval erupted on Thursday.
Earlier a Greek public prosecutor charged three senior officials of Delta Securities with fraud and banned them from leaving the country, court sources told Reuters.
Delta Securities was barred from trading on Thursday after failing to settle with the bourse clearing house, sending a shock wave through the market. Brokers reacted by boycotting trading.
Delta president Dimitris Argyriadis, vice-president Ioanna Gelestathi and board member Theofanis Gravanis were charged with large-scale, repeated fraud, the court sources said.
The case was assigned to an Athens investigating magistrate who will now hear testimony.

The general secretary of the national economy ministry, Antonis Fotiadis, predicted the bourse would operate normally on Monday and the settlement problem which shut down the exchange would be cleared up over the weekend.
Any shareholder losses from Delta Securities' settlement problem would be covered by the exchange's guarantee fund, he told reporters after meeting shareholder representatives.
He made clear that the state would not pick up the tab nor guarantee any future losses arising from settlement incidents.
The national economy ministry would consider legislative measures aimed at improving the operating mechanisms of the stock exchange and discourage regulatory violations.
Boycotting brokers said they were considering the matter and that no decision had been taken on whether to resume trading on Monday.
Several brokers said Fotiadis had done little to resolve the underlying problem and predicted there would be disagreement among brokers as to whether to resume trading on Monday.
The problems prompted bourse President Manolis Xanthakis to rush back from a conference in Hong Kong.
Government spokesman Dimitris Reppas said the bourse must sort out its own problems, however, and ruled out initiatives by the socialist government elected in September.
"The stock exchange, on its own, will face this problem and everything will go well," he said.
Market analysts expressed concerns about the problems triggering a domino effect, fearing more brokers might be overstretched on margin and short positions.

"The exchange authorities have been getting a lot more stringent with brokers on compliance issues. If the exchange presses too much some may have to declare bankruptcy," said ING Barings analyst Yannis Protopapadakis.
The clampdown may have opened a pandora's box of problems but, in the long run, it could make for a better market, others said. ($1=238.5 Drachma) --Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
